In [[mathematics]], and especially in [[order theory]], a '''nucleus'''  is a function <math>F</math> on a [[meet-semilattice]] <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> such that (for every <math>p</math> in <math>\mathfrak{A}</math>):<ref>{{citation|first=Peter|last=Johnstone|authorlink=Peter Johnstone (mathematician)|year=1982|title=Stone Spaces|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-33779-3|zbl=0499.54001|page=48|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CiWwoLNbpykC&pg=PA48}}</ref>

# <math>p \le F(p)</math>
# <math>F(F(p)) = F(p)</math>
# <math>F(p \wedge q) = F(p) \wedge F(q)</math>

Every nucleus is evidently a monotone function.

==Frames and locales==
Usually, the term ''nucleus'' is used in [[pointless topology]] (when the semilattice <math>\mathfrak{A}</math> is a frame).

'''Proposition:''' If <math>F</math> is a nucleus on a frame <math>\mathfrak{A}</math>, then the [[poset]] <math>\operatorname{Fix} F</math> of fixed points of <math>F</math>, with order inherited from <math>\mathfrak{A}</math>, is also a frame.<ref>{{cite book|title=An Introduction to Partially Ordered Structures and Sheaves|at=Theorem&nbsp;13.2, p.&nbsp;130|first=Francisco|last=Miraglia|publisher=Polimetrica s.a.s.|year=2006|isbn=9788876990359|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w6or65-Hw6UC&pg=PA130}}</ref>
